content: Serious and sometimes fatal hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported in patients undergoing penicillin therapy. While anaphylaxis is more commonly associated with parenteral administration, it has also occurred in patients taking oral penicillins. Individuals with a history of penicillin hypersensitivity or sensitivity to multiple allergens are at a higher risk of experiencing these reactions. Severe reactions have also been reported in patients with a history of penicillin hypersensitivity when treated with cephalosporins. Before initiating amoxicillin therapy, it is essential to thoroughly investigate any prior hypersensitivity reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, or other allergens. If an allergic reaction occurs, amoxicillin should be discontinued immediately, and appropriate treatment should be initiated. Severe anaphylactic reactions require emergency treatment with epinephrine, along with oxygen, intravenous steroids, and airway management, including intubation, as clinically indicated. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including amoxicillin. The severity of CDAD can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. Antibacterial therapy alters the normal flora of the colon, leading to an overgrowth of C. difficile, which produces toxins A and B that contribute to CDAD. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile are associated with increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may be resistant to antimicrobial therapy and may require colectomy. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use, even if it occurs up to two months after the last dose. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued. Appropriate fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, antibiotic treatment of C. difficile, and surgical evaluation should be implemented as clinically indicated. During amoxicillin therapy, the possibility of superinfections with fungal or bacterial pathogens should be considered. If superinfections occur, amoxicillin should be discontinued, and appropriate therapy should be initiated. A high percentage of patients with mononucleosis who receive ampicillin develop an erythematous skin rash. Therefore, ampicillin-class antibiotics, including amoxicillin, should not be administered to patients with mononucleosis. Amoxicillin should only be prescribed for proven or strongly suspected bacterial infections or for prophylactic indications. Unnecessary use increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Periodic assessment of renal, hepatic, and hematopoietic function is recommended during prolonged therapy with amoxicillin. Patients with gonorrhea should undergo serologic testing for syphilis at the time of diagnosis and follow-up testing after three months. Probenecid decreases the renal tubular secretion of amoxicillin, potentially leading to increased and prolonged blood levels of the drug. Concurrent use of amoxicillin with chloramphenicol, macrolides, sulfonamides, or tetracyclines may interfere with the bactericidal effects of penicillin, although the clinical significance of this interaction is not well-documented. Amoxicillin may alter gut flora, reducing estrogen reabsorption and potentially decreasing the efficacy of combined oral estrogen/progesterone contraceptives. High urine concentrations of ampicillin may result in false-positive reactions when testing for glucose in urine using certain methods (e.g., CLINITEST®, Benedict’s Solution, or Fehling’s Solution). Enzymatic glucose oxidase-based tests (e.g., Clinistix®) are recommended for accurate results. Transient decreases in plasma concentrations of total conjugated estriol, estriol-glucuronide, conjugated estrone, and estradiol have been observed following ampicillin administration in pregnant women, and this effect may also occur with amoxicillin. Long-term animal studies to evaluate the carcinogenic potential of amoxicillin have not been conducted. Mutagenicity studies of amoxicillin alone have not been performed, but a 4:1 mixture of amoxicillin and potassium clavulanate was non-mutagenic in bacterial and yeast assays. It was weakly positive in the mouse lymphoma assay at doses associated with decreased cell survival but negative in the mouse micronucleus test and dominant lethal assay. Potassium clavulanate alone was negative in mutagenicity tests. Reproductive studies in rats and mice at doses up to 10 times the human dose have shown no evidence of impaired fertility or harm to the fetus. However, there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Amoxicillin should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed. Oral ampicillin-class antibiotics are poorly absorbed during labor. Studies in guinea pigs have shown that intravenous ampicillin slightly decreases uterine tone and contraction frequency but moderately increases contraction height and duration. The effects of amoxicillin on labor and delivery in humans are unknown. Penicillins are excreted in human milk, and amoxicillin use by nursing mothers may lead to sensitization of infants. Caution is advised when administering amoxicillin to breastfeeding women. Due to immature renal function in neonates and young infants, amoxicillin elimination may be delayed, necessitating dosage adjustments in pediatric patients aged 12 weeks or younger (≤3 months). Clinical studies have not identified differences in responses to amoxicillin between elderly and younger patients. However, elderly patients are more likely to have decreased renal function, which may increase the risk of toxic reactions. Dose selection should be cautious, and renal function monitoring may be beneficial. Amoxicillin may be taken every 8 or 12 hours, depending on the prescribed product strength. Patients should be counseled that antibacterial drugs, including amoxicillin, should only be used to treat bacterial infections and not viral infections (e.g., the common cold). Patients should be advised to complete the full course of therapy as directed, even if they feel better early in the treatment. Skipping doses or not completing the therapy may reduce treatment effectiveness and increase the likelihood of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Diarrhea is a common side effect of antibiotics and usually resolves after discontinuation of the antibiotic. However, patients may develop watery and bloody stools (with or without stomach cramps and fever) even two or more months after completing antibiotic therapy. If this occurs, patients should contact their physician promptly.
